caveats: SQLite looks for matching child rows only on connections that enable PRAGMA foreign_keys; queries that join or filter on the key need the index either way.

fix.summary: Index the foreign key column on main.orders.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 43.9 s of database time over the 90 minutes the Rails log covers (99%). Deleting a row from main.customers, or changing its key, makes the database look for matching rows in main.orders (200K rows) without an index, which means reading the whole table. Queries that load orders rows for one customers row can't seek either. The statements that go through it take 99% of database time. SQLite already builds this index for itself on every run of one of these statements, and drops it after.
findings.title: orders has no index on customer_id, its foreign key to customers
verify: Explain the queries listed again: each reads main.orders through ix_orders_customer_id (`SEARCH … USING INDEX ix_orders_customer_id`) instead of reading all of it.
Re-scan once the index exists: this finding should be gone, and a delete from main.customers then finds the rows of main.orders it checks through the index, not by scanning the table.
Re-scan after the workload has run: the queries' time per run should drop.

findings.summary: Deleting a row from main.products, or changing its key, makes the database look for matching rows in main.order_items (200K rows) without an index, which means reading the whole table. Queries that load order_items rows for one products row can't seek either.
findings.title: order_items has no index on product_id, its foreign key to products
verify: Re-scan once the index exists: this finding should be gone, and a delete from main.products then finds the rows of main.order_items it checks through the index, not by scanning the table.

findings.summary: ix_orders_status_again has keys (status) and ix_orders_status has keys (status). They are the same index twice. Every write to main.orders maintains both.
findings.title: ix_orders_status_again duplicates ix_orders_status on orders
verify: Re-scan after removing ix_orders_status_again: this finding should be gone, and ix_orders_status should still exist.

Compare queries on main.orders over comparable periods before and after the change, under a similar workload: their time per run should stay the same or drop. If a query gets slower, check its plan before keeping the index removed.

fix.cost: ANALYZE reads every index once and holds the write lock while it stores the results: on a large file, run it when writes are quiet.
fix.summary: Run ANALYZE once, then PRAGMA optimize from time to time (when a connection closes is the usual place): it re-analyzes only what changed.

findings.summary: The file has no current sqlite_stat1 statistics, so SQLite falls back on fixed guesses about how big each table is and how well each index narrows a search. With 3 secondary indexes to choose from, a guess can pick the wrong one, or a full scan.
findings.title: SQLite has no statistics to choose between this file's indexes
verify: Scan again: the file has sqlite_stat1, and this finding is gone.

fix.cost: VACUUM holds the write lock for its whole run and can need up to twice the original file's size in free disk space.
fix.summary: VACUUM rewrites the file without its free pages. To give space back after large deletes from then on, switch auto_vacuum to INCREMENTAL first (it takes effect with that VACUUM) and run PRAGMA incremental_vacuum when convenient.

findings.summary: Deleted rows leave their pages in the file for SQLite to reuse; the file doesn't shrink on its own. That's fine when new rows will fill them again. If not, the file stays larger than its data, which every backup and copy pays for.
findings.title: 47.0 MB of the file is free pages (71% of it)
verify: Scan again: free pages are a small part of the file.
